Assignment 01 / Sculpting for Design

Tactile Topographies

A collection of surfaces, translated from the everyday world into the language of clay.

Observation · Sketching · Clay

The starting point was close observation: looking at textures that usually pass unnoticed, and asking how they might feel when drawn, pressed, or carved into a different material.

01

Looking a little closer

Medha began by observing natural and man-made textures around her. Bark, ground cover, patterned paving, and repeated geometric surfaces became a small library of marks. The interest lies in their differences: some textures are regular and constructed, while others are uneven, layered, or shaped by growth.

These photographs act as starting points rather than patterns to reproduce exactly. Each offers a different rhythm of lines, gaps, ridges, and small interruptions.

02

From surface to mark

The next step was to translate those observations into sketches. Drawing made it possible to isolate a texture from the object it belonged to: a surface could become hatching, a cluster of dots, or a repeated curved line.

Alongside the pencil studies, Medha assembled a visual collection of textures. Seen together, these studies show the movement from noticing a surface to deciding which of its qualities could be carried into clay.

03

A surface you can hold

The clay model brings several of these ideas onto one curved form. Different areas explore the flow of water leaving marks on a riverbed, the bark of a tree, and the roughness of moss and small pebbles.

Working around the vessel gives each texture its own space. Broad vertical channels sit beside smaller, repeated impressions; a rough band near the rim contrasts with the more deliberate marks below it. Turning the piece reveals a changing surface rather than one repeated pattern.

04

Observed, then imagined

The piece also includes invented textures made through hatching and dots. This is where the exercise moves beyond imitation: the surroundings supply a vocabulary, but the clay becomes a place to combine and extend it.

The resulting object records both observation and experimentation. Its interest is in the way a familiar sensation — flowing water, rough bark, pebbled ground — can be suggested through a different material.
